newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: U.S. ambassador slams Colombia extradition moves.
newsitem.headline: U.S. ambassador slams Colombia extradition moves.

text.p: Proposals by lawmakers to lift Colombia's ban on extradition will not help the country face up to its responsibility to combat drug trafficking, U.S. Ambassador Myles Frechette warned business leaders on Tuesday.

Frechette criticised the watered-down bill on extradition, approved in a first vote in the Senate last week, because it would not be applied retroactively -- slamming the door on U.S. efforts to take the jailed heads of the Cali drug cartel to stand trial in U.S. courts.

His comments set alarm bells ringing as legislators interpreted them as a sign Colombia would not regain its certification as a U.S. ally in the drug war, withdrawn in March over allegations that President Ernesto Samper was not doing enough to crack down on the cocaine trade.

"What has so far been approved in Congress (on extradition) doesn't really meet international requirements nor allow Colombia to face its responsibilities on organised crime," Frechette told a business association meeting.
He also raised doubts about the effectiveness of two other bills currently going through Congress to introduce stiffer penalties for drug traffickers.
National radio said Justice Minister Carlos Medellin had called in the ambassador to seek clarification on his comments but government sources were unable to confirm that.

One senator, Rodrigo Villalba, condemned Frechette's remarks as interventionist. "The ambassador should not pressure us. Those of us in favour of renewing extradition are not doing so because of U.S. pressure but as our own effort to tackle organised crime and drug trafficking," he said.

Colombia imposed a constitutional ban on extradition in 1991 after drug cartels waged a war of bombings, kidnaps and assassinations. The proposals now in Congress, which still face seven more votes, would not be retroactive nor apply to those traffickers who gave themselves up to Colombian justice.

Frechette's criticisms echoed similar those last week from chief prosecutor Alfonso Valdivieso, a fervent anti-drug crusader and a Washington favourite, who said the proposals were unworkable and represented no advance in the fight against drugs.
